title: The ENTIRE History of Japan in 10 Minutes
youtube_title: The ENTIRE History of Japan in 10 Minutes
description:
From the first rice farmers around 300 BC to the end of World War II in 1945, this is the whole story of Japan in about ten minutes: a legendary first emperor, a hidden queen, a temple-building company that lasted 1,400 years, one of the world's first novels, shoguns and samurai, Yasuke, 214 years behind a locked door, Perry's Black Ships and Japan's race to modernize. Every fact is checked, and legends are labelled as legends.

Chapters are added automatically.

#history #japan #samurai #japanesehistory #animatedhistory

beats.say: July 1853. Fishermen near Edo, the city we now call Tokyo, look out to sea and see something impossible.

show.place: Uraga Bay, near Edo, Japan · July 1853

beats.say: Four huge black ships glide into the bay against the wind. Two of them are pouring out smoke.
For over two hundred years, Japan had kept almost every foreigner out. Now Commodore Matthew Perry, an American navy officer, points his warships' guns at the shore.
Foreigners must go to Nagasaki. That's the only place we talk to them.
No, thanks. I'll deliver my letter right here.
Within fifteen years, the samurai government would collapse. Within about fifty, Japan would beat a European empire in a war. How did Japan get here? Let's go back.

show.text: The ENTIRE History of Japan in 10 Minutes

show.title: Rice, Legends and a Hidden Queen

beats.say: Japan is a chain of islands off the east coast of Asia. For thousands of years, people there lived by hunting, fishing and gathering.
Then, by about 300 BC, new ideas had arrived from the Asian mainland, including Korea. They brought rice farming, bronze and iron.
Rice changed everything. Rice needs teamwork. Teamwork needs bosses. And bosses, it turns out, need more bosses.
Japan's old royal chronicles say the first emperor was Jimmu, a descendant of the sun goddess. They say he took the throne in 660 BC.
Historians agree that's a legend. Those chronicles were written in the 700s AD, over thirteen hundred years later.
The first detailed written description of Japan comes from China. Chinese records tell of a queen called Himiko, who ruled around 240 AD. She led about thirty small states through religious power.
She was almost never seen. The records say only one man was allowed in, to bring her food and pass on her words.
May I meet the queen?
Nobody meets the queen. Tell me, and I'll tell her.

show.title: Buddhism and a Very Old Company

beats.say: In the 500s AD, Buddhism, a religion that began in India, reached Japan through Korea. Japan's rulers loved it, and wanted temples. Lots of temples.
According to the company's own history, in 578 builders from Korea were invited over to build a temple. One of them, Kongō Shigemitsu, started a family business.
Temples, shrines, castles. If it's wooden and holy, we fix it.
That business, Kongō Gumi, ran on its own for over fourteen hundred years. About forty generations of the same family led it.

show.label: Kongō Gumi ran on its own for
show.sub: 578 to 2006, then it joined a bigger firm

beats.say: It survived wars, fires and earthquakes. What finally beat it? It borrowed heavily in a 1980s land boom, then land prices crashed. A bigger company bought it in 2006.
Meanwhile, Japan copied China's style of government. It built grand capitals laid out like Chinese cities: Nara in 710, then Heian-kyō, today's Kyoto, in 794.

show.title: Poems, Silk and the First Novel

beats.say: Welcome to the Heian court. For its nobles, life was all about poems, silk robes and very, very long letters.
Around 1010, Murasaki Shikibu, an attendant to the empress, was writing a giant story. It was The Tale of Genji, about a charming prince and the people around him.
Is the next chapter ready yet?
Patience. There are fifty-four of them.
It has fifty-four chapters and about eight hundred poems, and it's often called the world's first novel. We don't even know the author's real name. Murasaki Shikibu is a nickname.
But while the nobles wrote poems, real power was slipping away to the countryside, to warriors called samurai.
Samurai were professional warriors who served lords in return for land. Two giant samurai clans, the Taira and the Minamoto, fought a huge war for control.
The Minamoto won. In 1192, their leader, Minamoto no Yoritomo, got the title shogun, meaning top military commander.

tag.text: Minamoto no Yoritomo, first Kamakura shogun

beats.say: Here's the twist. The emperor kept his throne, but the shogun ran the country. For almost seven hundred years, shoguns were the real bosses of Japan.
In 1274 and 1281, the Mongol rulers of China sent huge fleets to invade Japan. Samurai fought them off, and in 1281 a giant storm wrecked the fleet.
Then, from 1467, Japan shattered into more than a century of civil wars between warlords, local lords with their own armies. Historians call it the Warring States period.
In 1543, a storm blew a Chinese ship onto the small island of Tanegashima. On board were Portuguese traders, among the first Europeans ever to reach Japan.
Portugal is way over here, on the far western edge of Europe. Its ships had sailed all the way around Africa to trade in Asia.
The island's teenage lord, Tanegashima Tokitaka, bought two of their guns. They were matchlocks, early guns fired with a slow-burning cord. Japanese smiths copied them, and soon Japan made its own.
The warlord who used guns best was Oda Nobunaga. He was a ruthless, ambitious lord who set out to take over all of Japan.
In 1581, an African man arrived in Kyoto as a servant of Jesuit missionaries, Christian priests from Europe. Huge crowds shoved to see him.
Nobunaga had never seen anyone like him, and a Jesuit letter says he suspected ink.
That color must be painted on. Wash it off.
Scrub all you like, my lord. It's my skin.
Nobunaga was delighted and took him into service. Japanese records call him Yasuke, and say he got a house, money and a sword. Historians still argue whether that made him a true samurai.
Meanwhile, four Japanese Christian teenagers made the opposite trip. They sailed to Europe and met the Pope in Rome in 1585.
In 1582, one of Nobunaga's own generals turned on him, and Nobunaga died. His top general, Toyotomi Hideyoshi, a peasant's son, finished the job. By 1590, he had united Japan.

After Hideyoshi died in 1598, lords fought over his realm. In 1600, at the Battle of Sekigahara, several commanders switched sides mid-battle. That handed victory to Tokugawa Ieyasu, who became shogun three years later.
The Tokugawa shoguns wanted one thing: no more chaos. So they froze Japan in place.
They banned Christianity, threw out the Portuguese, and stopped Japanese people from traveling abroad. By 1639, Japan was almost completely closed.
Only Dutch and Chinese ships could still trade, at Nagasaki. The Dutch had to live on Dejima, a tiny artificial island in the harbor. It was about the size of two soccer fields.
That's how long Japan kept its door almost shut.

show.label: Japan mostly closed to the world

beats.say: Japan got over two hundred years of peace. Edo grew to over a million people, possibly the biggest city on Earth.

With no wars to fight, many samurai became paper-pushers, teachers and poets. One true story became Japan's favorite drama: in 1703, forty-seven ronin, samurai without a master, avenged their dead lord.

show.title: Black Ships and a Crash Course

beats.say: Then Perry showed up. A year later, the shogun's government signed a treaty opening two ports. Many Japanese were furious at the shogun for giving in.
In 1868, rebel lords overthrew the shogun and put the teenage Emperor Meiji back at the center. It's called the Meiji Restoration.
Their plan: learn everything from the West, fast. That way, foreign empires couldn't push Japan around, the way they were pushing China around.
In 1871, about fifty top officials set off on a huge study tour of America and Europe. They took notes on factories, schools and armies.
In 1872, Japan's first railway opened, from Tokyo to Yokohama. The emperor rode it himself.
And in 1876, samurai were banned from wearing their swords in public.
My family has worn these swords for generations!
Lovely. Now they can hang on your wall.
Some samurai rebelled in 1877, and lost to Japan's new army of drafted farmers. The age of the samurai was over.
Japan also started building an empire of its own. It took Taiwan in 1895, and later Korea.
Then, in 1904, it went to war with Russia. The Russian tsar sent his Baltic Fleet sailing halfway around the world to fight.
In May 1905, Admiral Tōgō destroyed it at the Battle of Tsushima. It was the first time in modern history an Asian power beat a European one in a major war.
Now the tone of our story has to change.
In the 1930s, military leaders took more and more control of Japan's government. In 1931, the army seized Manchuria in northeast China. In 1937, Japan launched a full-scale war on China.
That war brought terrible suffering. Millions of Chinese civilians died, including in the massacre at Nanjing.
In 1940, Japan signed an alliance with Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy.
On December 7, 1941, Japanese planes attacked the American naval base at Pearl Harbor, in Hawaii. More than two thousand four hundred Americans were killed.
The next day, President Franklin Roosevelt asked Congress to declare war on Japan, and it did.
Japan quickly conquered much of Southeast Asia and the Pacific. But from 1942 the tide turned, and American forces fought their way back, island by island.
On August 6, 1945, an American bomber dropped an atomic bomb on the city of Hiroshima. Three days later, a second one fell on Nagasaki.
By the end of that year, well over a hundred thousand people had died in the two cities.

show.label: Hiroshima and Nagasaki
show.sub: well over 100,000 dead by the end of the year

beats.say: On August 15, Emperor Hirohito spoke to his people on the radio. Ordinary Japanese had never heard an emperor's voice before. He told them Japan would accept the Allies' terms.
His most famous line is still quoted in Japan today.

show.text: ...by enduring the unendurable and suffering what is insufferable.

beats.say: On September 2, 1945, Japan formally surrendered aboard the battleship USS Missouri, in Tokyo Bay. The war was over.
In two thousand years, Japan went from rice paddies to shoguns to a modern industrial power. Then came one of history's darkest wars.
And one Japanese soldier didn't stop fighting until 1974. That story is in our shorts.
